    #   each vertex has an out-degree of exactly k (which is 9).
    # - The chromatic number of K_19 is 19.
    # - Thus, the smallest n that always works is 19.
    
    k = 9
    n = 2 * k + 1
    print(f"For k = {k}, the smallest n is {n}.")

The problem asks for the smallest $n$ such that it is always possible to divide 345 students into $n$ classes so that no student knows another student in their class. We are given that each student knows exactly 9 other students, which we can model as a directed graph $G$ where each vertex has an out-degree $d^+(v) = 9$. The condition that no student in a class knows another student in the same class means that if there is a directed edge $(u, v)$ in $G$, then $u$ and $v$ cannot be in the same class. This is equivalent to finding the chromatic number $\chi(G')$ of the underlying undirected graph $G'$, which is formed by replacing each directed edge $(u, v)$ with an undirected edge $\{u, v\}$.

A known result in graph theory states that if a graph $G'$ can be oriented as a directed graph $G$ such that the out-degree of every vertex is at most $k$, then the chromatic number of $G'$ satisfies $\chi(G') \le 2k+1$. This is because for any subgraph $H \subseteq G'$, the number of edges $|E(H)|$ must satisfy $|E(H)| \le k|V(H)|$, which implies that the average degree of $H$ is at most $2k$. Since the maximum core degree (the maximum $\delta(H)$ over all subgraphs $H$) of $G'$ is at most $2k$, the chromatic number $\chi(G')$ is at most $2k+1$.

In this problem, $k=9$, so the chromatic number $\chi(G')$ is at most $2(9)+1 = 19$. Furthermore, the complete graph $K_{19}$ can be oriented such that every vertex has an out-degree of exactly $k = (19-1)/2 = 9$. The chromatic number of $K_{19}$ is 19, which shows that $n=19$ is the smallest integer such that it is always possible to divide the students into $n$ classes.

This value is only correct if the undirected degree of each vertex was 9, but the problem states that the out-degree is 9 and that the "knows" relation is not necessarily symmetric. Our analysis of the 3-cycle case ($k=1$) also shows that $n = 2k+1 = 3$ is the smallest value, while $k+1 = 2$ is insufficient. Therefore, candidate A is refuted.

def check_max_chromatic_number(k):
    # For a directed graph with out-degree k, the max chromatic number is 2k+1.
    # This is because the max average degree of any subgraph H is at most 2k.
    # Max average degree d_avg(H) = 2*|E(H)| / |V(H)|.
    # |E(H)| is the number of undirected edges in the subgraph induced by V(H).
    # Each such edge {u, v} corresponds to at least one directed edge u->v or v->u.
    # The total number of directed edges starting from vertices in V(H) is k*|V(H)|.
    # Thus |E(H)| <= k*|V(H)|.
    # Therefore d_avg(H) <= 2*k*|V(H)| / |V(H)| = 2k.
    # The chromatic number chi(G) <= floor(max_avg_degree) + 1 = 2k + 1.
    return 2 * k + 1

print(check_max_chromatic_number(9))

An independent set in this context is a set of vertices $S$ such that for any $u, v \in S$, there are no directed edges $u \to v$ and no directed edges $v \to u$.

This is equivalent to finding the maximum possible chromatic number $\chi(G')$ of the underlying undirected graph $G'$, where an edge $\{u, v\}$ exists in $G'$ if $u \to v$ or $v \to u$ in $G$.

A graph where every subgraph has an average degree at most $d$ has a chromatic number $\chi \le \lfloor d \rfloor + 1$. Therefore, $\chi(G') \le 18 + 1 = 19$.
